title: The Human Skeleton
summary: How the 206 bones of the skeleton support the body, protect organs, work with muscles at joints, make blood, heal, and stay strong.
poll: Bones are just hard, lifeless parts of the body.

versions.title: Your Bones
versions.text:
Stand up tall. What holds you up? Your bones do! All of your bones make your skeleton.

A grown-up has 206 bones. A new baby has more. As the child grows, some bones join. They grow into one bone.

Bones keep you safe. Your skull is the hard bone in your head. It keeps your brain safe. Your ribs are like a cage. They guard your heart and lungs.

Your back has a long row of small bones. It is your spine. It lets you bend and twist.

The long bone in your leg is the biggest. The bone in your thigh is strong. The tiny bones in your ear are the smallest.

A joint is a spot where two bones meet. Your knee is a joint. So is your elbow.

Bones can not move on their own. A muscle pulls on a bone. Then the bone moves.

Bones are alive. Some make new blood. A bone that breaks can heal.

Bones need calcium to stay strong. Milk and cheese have it. Run and jump to help your bones, too!

Bones are alive. The soft part inside some bones makes new blood. A broken bone can heal.

Bones need calcium to stay strong. Milk, yogurt, and cheese have it. Running and jumping help your bones grow strong, too.

versions.title: The Bones Inside You
versions.text:
Stand up straight and stretch your arms toward the sky. What holds your body up? Your bones do! Together, all of your bones make up your skeleton. It works like the frame of a building, giving your body its shape.

An adult has 206 bones. A newborn baby actually has many more than that. As a child grows, some of the small bones join together, and they slowly become one larger bone.

Bones also protect the soft parts of your body. Your skull is the hard case around your head, and it keeps your brain safe. Your ribs form a curved cage that guards your heart and your lungs.

Your back has a long column of small bones called your spine. It holds you upright, but it still lets you bend, turn, and twist.

The thigh bone in your upper leg is the longest and strongest bone in your body. The tiny bones deep inside your ear are the smallest.

A joint is a place where two bones meet. Your knees, elbows, and fingers all have joints.

Bones cannot move by themselves. Each muscle is attached to bones, and when the muscle pulls, the bone moves.

Bones are living parts of your body. The soft center of some bones makes new blood cells. A broken bone can even heal itself.

Bones need calcium to stay strong. Milk, yogurt, and cheese contain plenty of it. Exercise such as running and jumping also makes your bones stronger.

versions.title: The Body's Living Frame
versions.text:
Stand up straight and stretch your arms toward the ceiling. What keeps your body from flopping onto the floor like a pile of laundry? The answer is your skeleton, the frame of bones that gives your body its shape and support.

An adult skeleton has 206 bones. Surprisingly, a newborn baby has many more, close to 300. As a child grows, some of those small bones fuse together, slowly becoming one larger, stronger bone.

Your skeleton does much more than hold you up. It also protects your soft organs. The skull is a hard case around your brain. Your ribs curve around your chest to form a cage that shields your heart and lungs.

Running down your back is the spine, a column of small bones called vertebrae. They are stacked like a tower of rings. The spine keeps you upright, yet it still lets you bend and twist.

The femur, or thigh bone, is the longest and strongest bone in your body. The smallest bone sits deep inside your ear and is about the size of a grain of rice.

Wherever two bones meet, there is a joint. Knees, elbows, and knuckles are all joints. Bones cannot move on their own, so muscles do the work. When a muscle tightens, it pulls on a bone and moves it.

Bones are living tissue. Inside many bones is a soft material called marrow, which makes new blood cells every day. Because bones are alive, a broken bone can slowly heal.

To stay strong, bones need calcium, which is found in milk, yogurt, and cheese. Exercise such as running and jumping also builds stronger bones.

versions.title: Inside the Human Skeleton
versions.text:

That hidden structure is your skeleton, the remarkable framework of bones that gives the body its shape and provides support for every other system.

An adult skeleton contains 206 bones. Surprisingly, a newborn baby possesses considerably more, approximately 300, and as a child develops, many of those small bones gradually fuse together, forming single larger and sturdier bones.

The skeleton accomplishes far more than holding a person upright, because it also protects delicate internal organs. The skull forms a rigid case around the brain, while the ribs curve around the chest to create a protective cage that shields the heart and lungs from injury.

To remain strong, bones require calcium, a mineral found in milk, yogurt, and cheese. Regular physical activity, such as running and jumping, also encourages the body to build denser, healthier bones.

The skeleton additionally stores this mineral, releasing it into the bloodstream whenever other organs require it. Regular physical activity, such as running and jumping, encourages the body to construct denser, healthier bones that resist injury throughout adulthood.

questions.stem: What is this article mostly about?
options: How to fix a broken arm at home
The bones in our body and what they do
Why milk is the best drink
How babies learn to walk
questions.why: The whole article tells how bones hold us up, protect us, move with muscles, stay alive, and stay strong.

wrong.A: The article says a broken bone can heal, but it does not tell how to fix one at home.
wrong.C: Milk is one small detail about calcium.
wrong.D: The article does not talk about babies learning to walk.

wrong.A: The number in the article is 206, not 106.
wrong.B: A baby has more bones than a grown-up, but 300 is not the grown-up number.
wrong.D: The article does not give 26 as the number of bones.

wrong.C: The ear bones are the smallest bones; they do not guard the heart.
wrong.D: The thigh bone is in the leg.

options: a muscle makes blood
food turns into calcium
the brain sits
two bones meet

wrong.B: Calcium comes from food; a joint is not about food.

questions.stem: What happens when a muscle pulls on a bone?
options: The bone breaks.
The bone moves.
The bone gets smaller.
The bone turns into two bones.

wrong.C: Nothing in the article says bones shrink when pulled.
wrong.D: Bones join as a child grows; they do not split when muscles pull.

options: Grown-ups lose bones when they fall.
Babies eat more cheese.
Some small bones join as a child grows.
Babies have an extra skull.
questions.why: The article says some small bones join and grow into one bone as a child grows, so the number goes down.

wrong.B: Food is not the reason for the number of bones.
wrong.D: Everyone has one skull.

questions.stem: Why does the article say that bones are alive?
options: Bones can see and hear.
Bones can make blood and heal.
Bones move without muscles.
Bones never change.

wrong.A: Bones do not see or hear.
wrong.C: The article says bones cannot move without muscles.
wrong.D: Bones do change: they grow, join, and heal.

questions.stem: Why does the author end the article with milk, cheese, running, and jumping?
options: To tell readers how to keep their bones strong
To list the author's favorite foods
To explain how the skull works
To show that sports can break bones
questions.why: The last part gives tips for strong bones: eat foods with calcium and be active.

wrong.B: The foods are there because they have calcium, not because the author likes them.
wrong.C: The skull is in an earlier part of the article.
wrong.D: The ending says running and jumping help bones; it is not about injuries.

LOW.prompt: Name two jobs your skeleton does for you. Use facts from the article to explain each job.
checklist: I used at least two facts from the article.
I wrote complete sentences with capital letters and periods.
LOW.modelAnswer: One job of my skeleton is to protect my body, because my skull covers my brain like a hard case and my ribs curve around my heart and lungs. Another job is to help me move, because muscles pull on bones at a joint, like my knee or elbow, so I can bend and walk. My skeleton also needs calcium from foods like milk and cheese to stay strong.

MID.prompt: Explain how bones and muscles work together to help you move. Use details from the article.
checklist: I used at least two facts from the article.
I wrote complete sentences with capital letters and periods.
MID.modelAnswer: Bones cannot move by themselves, so muscles do the actual work of moving the skeleton. When a muscle tightens, it pulls on a bone at a joint, such as the knee or elbow, and that pull makes the bone move. This happens with bones all over the body, including the femur, the longest and strongest bone, which muscles pull on every time I take a step. Even the small vertebrae in my spine can bend and twist because muscles pull on them one at a time.

questions.stem: Based on the article, what might happen if a person's diet had too little calcium for a long time?
options: Their bones could become weaker.
Their body would grow extra ribs to protect the heart and lungs.
Their ligaments would turn into bone.
Their marrow would stop being soft.

questions.stem: Why is it helpful that the spine is made of many vertebrae instead of one long bone?

Many small bones let the back bend and twist while staying upright.
Vertebrae are the only bones with marrow.
A single bone could not hold ligaments.
questions.why: The article says the spine keeps the body upright while still allowing it to bend, rotate, and twist, which a single rigid bone could not do.

HIGH.prompt: The article calls the skeleton a 'living framework.' Explain what this phrase means, using at least two pieces of evidence from the text.
checklist: I used at least two facts from the article.
I wrote complete sentences with capital letters and periods.
HIGH.modelAnswer: Calling the skeleton a living framework means that it is not just a stiff structure like a building frame, but a framework made of tissue that is actually alive and always changing. For example, the article explains that bones contain marrow, which produces millions of new blood cells every single day, proving that bones are active rather than lifeless. The skeleton also keeps changing as a person grows, since nearly 300 small bones in a newborn gradually fuse together into the 206 sturdier bones of an adult. Because the bones are alive, they can even repair themselves after a break, which no simple framework of sticks could ever do.
